transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Head of Search, Mosaic), Tom Reyes (Platform Eng), Priya Menon (Data Scientist)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, and with me is Samir, our SE. We just want to get a sense of your current retrieval + rerank pipeline and where we can help.
[00:04] Aisha: Hi, yes thanks. Quick intro — Mosaic Insights, we power relevance for a B2B research product, lots of daily queries, roughly 120 million qps per month? uh monthly queries, user traffic spikes are really bursty.
[00:10] Tom: Sorry, to clarify — 120M queries per month, peak concurrent QPS around mid tens of thousands depending on campaign windows.
[00:17] Priya: We currently run an in-house vector store on k8s backed by NVMe nodes, and we do a hybrid approach: ANN topK from our VDB then a model rerank using a 7B cross-encoder on GPU endpoints.
[00:26] Samir: Okay got it. When you say "in-house VDB" are you managing sharding, replication, and tail latency yourselves?
[00:30] Priya: Yeah. Tom's team handles shards, but we've started hitting tail latency problems when fanout is high — like when we try multi-field retrieval or faas style queries.
[00:38] Jordan: Perfect. One of the things we've seen is customers trade embedding dimension and model size to reduce cost at the embedding stage, then rely on rerank for final accuracy. Curious if that's something you've evaluated.
[00:46] Aisha: We've tried 768 vs 1536 dims. 1536 gives better recall but doubles vector size and storage, and the VDB lookup latency increased slightly. We also looked at int8 quantized embeddings to save space but accuracy dip worried us.
[00:56] Tom: The big ask is predictable tail latency under heavy fanout. If we do a 50 shard fanout to get recall, our 95th gets pretty bad. Also, we want minimum operational overhead — not running one-off kernel tuning and all that.
[01:06] Samir: Makes sense. High-level, Redwood can be used as hosted API for quick rollout, Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) for predictable throughput, or Private (VPC or on-prem) for network-isolated setups. For heavy fanout combined with rerank, we typically recommend a hybrid where the VDB handles ANN retrieval and Redwood serves rerank or a second-phase rerank with a compact candidate generator in Redwood.
[01:20] Priya: When you say hybrid, do you mean our VDB stays primary and Redwood is just the reranker? Or can Redwood also host the approximate nearest neighbor lookup?
[01:26] Samir: Both are possible. If you want minimal change, keep your VDB and call Redwood for rerank. If you want us to handle embedding and retrieval, we can run a vector index inside Dedicated/Private and manage sharding and KV cache optimizations to reduce per-request work. There's a middle ground where embeddings are computed in Redwood but indexed in your VDB with prefix caching on common queries.
[01:40] Aisha: Interesting. Our infra team is nervous about sending vectors out to hosted APIs for PII reasons, so Private or Dedicated is more likely.
[01:46] Jordan: Totally reasonable. For Private we support customer-managed VPC and can integrate with your KMS for encryption at rest. We also have SOC2 material and network diagrams — we'll share that.
[01:53] Tom: On the rerank model — we run a 7B cross-encoder single-GPU per replica. The cost there is high. How do you manage autoscaling for the reranker during traffic spikes?
[01:59] Samir: For Dedicated, you reserve a pool and we can configure autoscale policies and burst capacity. The serving runtime does continuous batching and smart token-level batching which reduces per-request compute. For Private, similar tooling applies but you're responsible for autoscaling infra unless we manage it.
[02:12] Priya: Can the reranker be quantized? We care about latency but also quality.
[02:15] Samir: Yes, we support quantized model variants. There are tradeoffs; for cross-encoders we commonly recommend int8 or int4 mixed with calibration for minimal regressed metrics. We also recommend running small eval prompt sets to measure MRR/precision drop before rolling out.
[02:26] Aisha: Great. Let's talk throughput. For our peak windows we need about 30k candidate+rerank qps sustained for 20 minutes. Average candidate size is 200 candidates per query before rerank.
[02:36] Jordan: 30k qps times 200 candidates is big — are those candidates per second or per user query?
[02:40] Priya: Per user query. So yes, that multiplies quickly. We actually do a two-stage: ANN top1k then micro-rerank to top 50 and final cross-encoder. That 200 number was a simplification.
[02:49] Tom: Also, not every query needs full rerank. About 60% use the fast heuristic rerank. The remaining 40% do the full cross-encoder. We want Redwood to be smart about routing to cheaper variants when appropriate.
[02:58] Samir: We support policy-based routing — you can route by latency SLO, cost, or a sample flag. There's also automatic fallback to cheaper model variants when Dedicated capacity is saturated.
[03:06] Aisha: On the vector DB side, what's the recommended dimensionality if using Redwood end-to-end? We want to reduce storage but keep recall.
[03:11] Samir: It depends on embedding model. For many workloads, 768 dims with a stronger reranker hits a good cost/quality point. For specialized similarity, 1536 sometimes needed. We can run an eval sweep using your dataset to recommend dims and quantization.
[03:21] Priya: We'll definitely want that. Also curious about index type — HNSW vs IVF+PQ — we currently run HNSW but it's memory hungry.
[03:28] Samir: We support multiple index strategies. For Dedicated/Private we can tune PQ/IVF to reduce memory footprint and accept a controlled recall tradeoff. HNSW is lower latency but higher RAM; PQ reduces index size but can increase tail latency for cold queries.
[03:39] Jordan: Question for Tom: how strict are your compliance requirements? You mentioned PII — is data residency a factor?
[03:44] Tom: For now it's internal PII rules, not legal residency. So VPC + KMS + audit logs are must-haves. SOC2 would be nice.
[03:50] Jordan: We'll attach our SOC2 report and explain audit log retention options.
[03:53] Aisha: Another operational question — how do you handle KV cache and prefix caching? Some of our queries are almost identical; we want to avoid repeated rerank costs.
[03:59] Samir: Our runtime supports KV cache at the token and prefix levels; for retrieval we also support candidate-level caching so if a candidate set repeats we can skip rerank entirely or use a cached rerank score. That reduces per-token cost substantially for repetitive queries.
[04:11] Priya: How do you measure cost? We currently bill by CPU/GPU hours and NVMe IOPS for the VDB. We're interested in token-level and per-embedding unit costs to compare unit economics.
[04:19] Jordan: Hosted is usage-based (per-token/per-embedding). Dedicated is reserved capacity with commit tiers and lower unit price plus SLA. Private is license+support with optional managed services. We'll send a cost comparison for your traffic profile.
[04:29] Tom: Performancewise, can you share any numbers for tail latency for rerank at high QPS? Our 95th is scary — 1.2s during spikes.
[04:36] Samir: Typical Dedicated setups we've worked with hit 95th under 200-300ms for cross-encoder rerank at high scale when combined with batching and smart sharding, but it depends on batchability of requests and sequence lengths. If you can provide sample queries we'll run a bench on our infra and simulate.
[04:48] Aisha: We'll share traces. One more thing: what about consistency between VDB and Redwood index if we index in two places? We want eventual consistency guarantees, not staleness for search results.
[04:56] Samir: If you index separately, we recommend a single source of truth for writes and a sync pipeline with sequence numbers. For near-real-time, the recommendation is to stream updates to Redwood's indexer and to your VDB; we provide hooks to ensure ordering and can surface lag metrics in Console.
[05:10] Priya: Good. On fallbacks: if Dedicated is overloaded, what's the failure mode? Do you route to hosted or degrade quality?
[05:16] Samir: Policies are configurable — automatic fallback to hosted with reduced model size, or graceful degradation where we return cached results. You can set fail-open or fail-closed behaviors per route.
[05:24] Tom: Network wise, if we go Private with our VPC, how do agents like Redwood reach our endpoints? Is there a connector or do we run agents?
[05:31] Samir: For Private we provide a customer-managed control plane; most customers use peering or private link. For air-gapped on-prem, we have a bundle you deploy; for VPC there is a lightweight agent for metrics and health that runs in your VPC.
[05:42] Aisha: Pricing aside, what's the typical pilot? How do we validate performance safely?
[05:47] Jordan: Pilot path we recommend: 1) dry-run bench with sample traffic on Redwood Dedicated to validate tail latency and cost, 2) small production shadowing for a percent of traffic, 3) gradual rollout with canary and evals. We'll provide a benchmark template and runbook.
[05:59] Priya: On evals — can Redwood tie regressions to prompt sets? We want to monitor MRR and surface regression alerts if we change quantization or dims.
[06:05] Samir: Yes, Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to your eval prompt sets. We can integrate those into your CI to gate rollouts.
[06:12] Tom: A question on embedding pipelines — do you recommend computing embeddings at ingest or at query time? We currently do ingest-time embeddings but with reindex windows there's delay.
[06:20] Priya: We also do incremental reindexing. The problem is when models change and we need to re-embed millions of docs.
[06:25] Samir: For most customers, ingest-time embeddings are recommended for read-latency; for model rollouts you can do bulk re-embedding in batches and use blue/green indexing. Redwood's Console can manage model versioning and coordinate rollouts.
[06:35] Aisha: Ok, this is helpful. Internal stakeholders to loop in are our Security lead and Platform lead.
[06:40] Jordan: Who will be the decision maker on hosting — security or platform?
[06:43] Aisha: Security will sign off on Private vs Dedicated. Platform wants Dedicated for manageability, but Security's comfort will decide.
[06:49] Tom: Timeline — we're aiming to pick a vendor and start pilot in 6-8 weeks. Budget is TBD but we'll probably do a 3-month pilot.
[06:55] Jordan: Sounds doable. We'll get the benchmark sheet and SOC2 docs over this week. Samir, can you run a sizing sketch based on their numbers?
[07:01] Samir: Yep — I'll draft a sizing for Dedicated and an estimated cost for hosted. I'll also outline index strategies (HNSW vs IVF+PQ) and recommend embedding dims.
[07:08] Priya: We'll provide a 24-hour trace and sample docs.
[07:12] Jordan: Great. Any other questions?
[07:15] Aisha: Just one — do you have references for customers who moved from in-house VDB to Redwood for rerank?
[07:19] Jordan: Yes, we can share anonymized case studies — I'll include those links.
[07:22] Tom: Thanks.
[07:23] [wrap-up]
[07:24] Jordan: Quick recap: Jordan to send pricing/benchmark template and SOC2 + network diagrams. Samir to send sizing and indexing recommendations. Mosaic to share traces and sample queries. Schedule deep technical dive next week.
[07:37] End of meeting.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mislabels and missed punctuation. Some technical terms transcribed as separate letters (e.g., K V cache).

References mentioned: Redwood Console, Redwood Optimize, Dedicated capacity, Private VPC options, KV cache, HNSW, IVF+PQ, int8/int4 quantization, cross-encoder rerank, candidate-level caching.

Shared artifacts: "throughput-benchmark-template.xlsx" (linked in notes), "SOC2-redwood.pdf" (to be shared), sizing sketch (to be produced by Samir).
